source.title_on_document: An empirical investigation of the impact of ChatGPT on creativity

paper_design_summary: Six online experiments (Experiments 1, 2A, 2B, 3, 4, 5) with MTurk or Prolific participants in the USA. Participants were randomly assigned to use ChatGPT (GPT-3.5), Google Web search, or no aid (Human-only) to produce one creative idea (several allowed in Experiment 1) for everyday problems: a toy from given items, repurposing household items, a new dining table, a gift for a teenage girl. Separate crowd judges rated each idea on originality and appropriateness (averaged into a creativity score), and three expert judges rated the ideas as a robustness check; Experiment 2B adds 100 raw ChatGPT-only responses as a non-randomized AI-output arm.

eligibility.reason: All six experiments randomly assign individual online participants to ChatGPT versus Google Web search and/or a no-aid Human-only arm (Methods, PDF pp. 6-8), analyze 194 to 400 people each, and score each submitted idea on creativity by crowd and expert judges. Experiment 2B also contains a non-randomized ChatGPT-only arm (100 raw GPT-3.5 responses) whose contrast with Human-only is ai_vs_human context. Arm-level participant counts are not reported in any experiment.

one_line_finding: Across six online experiments, ideas produced with ChatGPT were rated more creative than ideas produced with Google search (d = 0.32 to 1.01) or with no aid (d = 0.56 in Experiment 2A, 1.88 in Experiment 2B), Table 1, PDF p. 5 (journal p. 1910).
open_questions: Arm-level and cell-level participant counts are not printed for any experiment; they may be in the OSF data (https://osf.io/rzn87/).
Experiment 2B ChatGPT-only s.d. is 0.40 in Table 1 and the first Results mention but 0.30 in the ChatGPT-assisted versus ChatGPT-only comparison (PDF p. 3).

Experiment 2B: the Reporting Summary (PDF p. 11) attributes the G*Power power analysis to Experiment 2A, while Methods (PDF p. 7) attributes it to Experiment 2B; the Data exclusions line gives no count for 2B although 216 finished and 200 were analyzed.

Experiment 4: Table 1 labels the fourth row 'ChatGPT-assisted x Low constraints' where the text (PDF p. 4) gives it as the Web-search-assisted low-constraint cell (4.40, s.d. 0.61). The ANOVA main effect F1,396 = 5.06 looks small next to the two simple-effect t-values (2.25 and 2.40); not resolved from the document.
Experiment 3 judges are described with the same mean age and percent female as the participants (43.11 years; 50 percent female), PDF pp. 3 and 7; possibly a copy error.
Experiment 1 Methods report P = 0.149 for t231 = 1.42 on the number of ideas (PDF p. 6).
Expert-judge results for Experiment 2B, and the sub-dimension analyses for Experiments 2A-5 (Supplementary Notes E and G), are not in this PDF.
notes: The paper reports no diversity or similarity outcome across participants, so it answers only with_ai. Outcome units: in Experiments 1, 2A, 3, 4, 5 the t-test degrees of freedom equal participants analyzed minus the number of cells (Experiment 1 averages each participant's idea scores), so unit = participant; in Experiment 2B the error df of 297 reflects 200 people plus 100 ChatGPT-only responses, so unit = output with n_units = 300. Arm means and s.d.s are printed, but arm ns are not, so 'arm_means_sds_ns' is not checked. Lay judges were recruited from the same panel as participants (MTurk n = 331, 158; Prolific n = 232, 241, 321, 310); expert judges were three professionals in every experiment. Outcomes not coded as separate rows: Experiment 3 self-reported idea exposition aid and other self-reports (not scored on output); serial mediation indirect effects (0.11, 95% CI (0.01, 0.22); experts 0.20, 95% CI (0.09, 0.34)); Experiment 2B correlation of self-reported modification with creativity (r = 0.11, P = 0.291); Experiment 1 share of top-ranked ideas (Supplementary Note F, not in this PDF). The paper also mentions a lay survey (n = 100) and a pilot survey (Supplementary Notes A and B) that measure attitudes only. Not from this document: the codebook (section 2) states that Meincke, Nave, and Terwiesch (2025) reanalyzes the participants of Lee and Chung (2024); this paper itself reanalyzes no other paper's sample. PDF page numbers: PDF pp. 1-9 = journal pp. 1906-1914; PDF pp. 10-12 = Reporting Summary.
